Physiognomy means one of two closely related things: either the face and its features, or the belief/practice of judging someone's character by looking at their face. These two meanings are deeply connected, and understanding both will give you the full picture.

In its most straightforward sense, physiognomy simply refers to a person's face — specifically, their facial features as a whole, considered together. It's a more formal or literary way of saying "face" or "facial appearance."

If someone says, "He had the physiognomy of a kind man," they mean his face — the shape of it, the way his features were arranged — gave the impression of kindness.

It's often used to describe a face that is distinctive, expressive, or character-filled. Writers especially love this word because it captures not just what a face looks like, but what it seems to say about a person.
Meaning 2: The Practice of Reading Character from Faces

This is the older, deeper, and more loaded meaning of the word.

Physiognomy is the idea — and the practice built around that idea — that you can figure out what a person is like on the inside by studying the features of their face. Their honesty, their intelligence, their cruelty or warmth — all supposedly revealed by the shape of their jaw, the distance between their eyes, the curve of their forehead, or the set of their mouth.

Think of it as a kind of face-reading — not mystical like palmistry, but dressed up in the language of observation and science. For centuries, people genuinely believed that nature had written a person's soul onto their face, and that a trained eye could read it.

For example, a practitioner of physiognomy might have claimed:

  • A high, broad forehead = intelligence
  • Small, close-set eyes = untrustworthiness
  • A strong, square jaw = determination and courage
  • A weak or receding chin = cowardice or lack of willpower

Yes — very much so, for a very long time.

Physiognomy wasn't considered fringe or odd. For centuries, from ancient times through to the 1800s, it was treated as a legitimate field of knowledge. Educated people studied it. Books were written about it. Judges, employers, and even doctors used it to form opinions about people.

The 18th-century Swiss pastor Johann Kaspar Lavater wrote enormously popular books on physiognomy that were read across Europe and taken seriously by intellectuals of the time.

Today, however, physiognomy is considered a pseudoscience — meaning it looks like science on the surface, but has no real scientific foundation. There is no credible evidence that the shape of someone's nose or the spacing of their eyes reveals anything about their character. Modern science has thoroughly rejected it.

This matters because physiognomy was also used to justify deeply harmful prejudices. When you classify people's worth or character based on their physical appearance, it becomes a tool for discrimination, racism, and cruelty. This is a dark part of the word's history that you should be aware of.
A Third, Extended Meaning: The "Face" of a Place or Thing

By extension, physiognomy can also describe the overall characteristic appearance of something that isn't a person — most commonly a landscape, a city, a region, or an era.

In this sense, it means the distinctive outward "face" or visible character of something, the features that make it look the way it looks and give it its particular identity.

For example:

  • "The physiognomy of the town had changed beyond recognition after the development boom." → The overall visible appearance and character of the town had changed.
  • "The physiognomy of the landscape shifts dramatically as you drive from the coast into the mountains." → The characteristic appearance of the land transforms.

This usage borrows from the personal meaning: just as a face is the outward expression of a person, the "physiognomy" of a place is its outward expression — the visual features that define its identity and mood.
How to Recognize It in Sentences

Here are some ways you'll see this word used in real writing, across all its meanings:

  • "From his physiognomy alone, she couldn't tell whether he was a man to be trusted." → His face/facial features.
  • "Medieval physiognomy held that a man with a thin upper lip was born without mercy." → The belief/practice.
  • "The physiognomy of the industrial city — its grey skies, its smoke-stained buildings — reflected its history." → The outward appearance of a place.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

What it literally isA formal/literary noun referring to the face, or the supposed art of reading character from faces
Meaning 1A person's face and facial features, especially as expressions of character
Meaning 2The historical practice of judging inner character from outer facial features (now a discredited pseudoscience)
Meaning 3The overall visible appearance or "face" of a place, landscape, or era
Tone of the wordFormal, literary, intellectual — not everyday casual language

Physiognomy means either a person's face and its characteristic features, or the old belief and practice that a person's face reveals their inner character — and by extension, it can also mean the distinctive outward appearance of a place or landscape.
